title: I have called you friends (John 15:15)

cards: There's a difference between an employee and a friend, and you can hear it in what you're told. An employee gets instructions: do this by Friday, here's the form. Whether they understand why is optional.
A friend gets the story: here's what's going on, here's what I'm worried about, here's why it matters. The tasks might even be the same. What's different is whether you're let in.
At the supper, Jesus tells the people at the table which one they are.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "I will not now call you servants: for the servant knoweth not what his lord doth. But I have called you friends: because all things whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you."
Notice the reason he gives. Not because you've earned it, or because you're equals.
Because I've told you everything. Friendship, here, means being let in on what the Father is doing. Servant in the Greek is doulos, often meaning a slave, someone who simply carries out orders.
Being called God's servant was already an honor in the scriptures: Moses was called the servant of the Lord. But there's an older word too.
Abraham was called the friend of God, in Isaiah and again in the letter of James. Jesus offers that same title to a table of fishermen and a tax collector. He doesn't drop the commands.
The verse just before says, you are my friends if you do the things I command you. Friends still do what's asked. They just know why.
This picture runs deep in the way many Catholics pray.
Saint Teresa of Ávila, the sixteenth-century Carmelite, described mental prayer as close, friendly conversation, often alone, with the one we know loves us.
Not a speech to a distant king. A conversation with a friend who has already told you his secrets: the move from following orders to being let in.

how: Many Catholics practice mental prayer, an unscripted conversation with God, often in silence before the tabernacle, alongside the set prayers of the Church.

games.q: you've worked for someone for three years. tonight, instead of instructions, they tell you everything they're planning and why. what has changed?
games.why: Jesus says it straight out: I have called you friends, because all things I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you.

practice: Sit the way you would across from someone you trust, and instead of formal words, say plainly, inside, what today has actually been like: what went well, what's bothering you, what you're not sure about.
If you pray, say it to God the way Teresa described, as to a friend who loves you; if you don't, tell it to the quiet, honestly. Then listen for a while.

wordCard.voice: Friends. Jesus at the supper: not servants who only get orders, but friends who've been told everything. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: friends (John 15:15), set against douloi, servants.

carryVoice: Your line: friends, not servants. Let in on the story, not just handed the task. Day five hundred twenty-two.
